chapter.name: Symmetry
chapter.blurb: Line and rotational symmetry of plane figures: finding lines of symmetry by folding, generating symmetric shapes through ink-blot folding, paper cutting and punching, angles of symmetry and the centre/order of rotation for radial-arm figures and regular polygons, and the special case of a circle's infinite symmetry.

scope_in.item: Test whether a line is a line of symmetry by folding a figure along it and checking that the two parts overlap exactly
Find all the lines of symmetry of a square by folding it vertically, horizontally and along both diagonals (4 lines in total)
Recognise that a rectangle's diagonal is a line of symmetry only when the rectangle is a square
Reflection: track where each labelled corner of a figure (e.g. square ABCD) moves when reflected along a given line of symmetry, and that this is also called giving the figure reflection symmetry

Generate and analyse symmetric figures using ink-blot folding, paper folding-and-cutting, and punching holes in folded paper, including predicting the number/position of holes and reconstructing how the paper was folded from a punched pattern
Count the lines of symmetry of triangles: an equilateral triangle has 3, an isosceles (non-equilateral) triangle has 1, a scalene triangle has 0, and no triangle can have exactly 2 lines of symmetry
Rotational symmetry: rotate a figure about a fixed centre of rotation and identify whether it looks unchanged at some angle strictly between 0 degrees and 360 degrees
Every figure has 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry, whether or not it has rotational symmetry
Find the angles of symmetry of a square (90 degrees, 180 degrees, 270 degrees, 360 degrees) by tracking its corners under rotation
Find the angles of symmetry of a figure with n equally spaced radial arms as the n multiples of 360 degrees divided by n
The angles of symmetry of a figure are whole-number multiples of its smallest angle of symmetry; the total number of angles of symmetry a figure has is its order of rotational symmetry
Decide whether a given whole number of degrees can be a figure's smallest angle of symmetry by checking whether it is a factor of 360 degrees
Symmetries of a circle: every angle is an angle of symmetry and every diameter is a line of symmetry
A regular polygon with n equal sides and angles has n lines of symmetry

Identify lines and angles of symmetry in real objects such as the Ashoka Chakra (24 spokes give 24 lines and 24 angles of symmetry) and the outer boundary of the New Parliament Building (3 lines of symmetry; rotational symmetry angles 120 degrees, 240 degrees, 360 degrees)

scope_out.item: Planes of symmetry of 3-D solids, such as a cube or a cone
scope_out.reason: This chapter treats only flat, plane figures; no solid shapes are discussed

scope_out.item: Translational symmetry, point symmetry, or any named symmetry type other than line (reflection) symmetry and rotational symmetry
scope_out.reason: The chapter names only these two kinds of symmetry; no other symmetry vocabulary appears

scope_out.item: Reflecting a point using coordinates on a graph, e.g. reflecting (x, y) about the x-axis or y-axis
scope_out.reason: All symmetry here is found by physical folding, cutting and tracing on paper, never by plotting coordinates

scope_out.item: Formal transformation vocabulary such as translation, glide reflection, or composition of transformations
scope_out.reason: Not used anywhere in this chapter

scope_out.item: Deriving or extending the Regular Polygons and Koch Snowflake number sequences referenced from Chapter 1, Table 3
scope_out.reason: Exercises point back to Chapter 1 for the sequences themselves; this chapter only asks students to count lines/angles of symmetry of shapes already given, not to build the sequences
Formal geometric construction is Chapter 8, 'Playing with Constructions'; this chapter builds symmetric figures only by paper folding, cutting, punching and grid tracing

scope_out.item: A rigorous proof that the angles of symmetry must be whole-number multiples of the smallest angle
scope_out.reason: The chapter presents this only as an observed pattern confirmed by a True/False check (p. 236), not as a derived theorem

concepts.name: Line of symmetry
concepts.description: A line that divides a figure into two mirror-image halves that exactly overlap when folded along it.
concepts.idea: Folding along a true line of symmetry makes the two halves match perfectly, like a mirror reflection.
concepts.rule: A line that cuts a figure into two parts that exactly overlap when folded along it is called a line of symmetry (or axis of symmetry) of the figure; not every line drawn through a figure works.
concepts.example: A blue triangle folded along a dotted line has its two halves match exactly, so the dotted line is a line of symmetry; a four-piece puzzle folded along another dotted line does not match, so that line is not a line of symmetry.

questions.q: A line that cuts a figure into two parts that exactly overlap when folded along it is called a
questions.a: line of symmetry

questions.q: Another name for a line of symmetry is an ____ of symmetry.
questions.a: axis

questions.q: When a figure is folded along its line of symmetry, the two halves
questions.a: overlap exactly

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a requirement for a line to be a line of symmetry of a figure?
questions.a: the line must be either exactly vertical or exactly horizontal
o: the line must be either exactly vertical or exactly horizontal
folding along it must make the two parts overlap exactly
the two parts on either side of the line must be mirror images
the line must divide the figure into two parts

questions.q: A square piece of paper is folded along one of its diagonals and the two triangular halves overlap exactly. What can we conclude about that diagonal?
questions.a: it is a line of symmetry of the square
o: it is a line of symmetry of the square
it is not a line of symmetry
it works only if the square is rotated first

questions.q: A rectangle that is not a square is folded along its diagonal; the two halves do ____ overlap exactly.
questions.a: not

questions.q: The diagonal of which shape is always a line of symmetry?
questions.a: a square
o: a rectangle that is not a square

questions.q: A kolam (rangoli) pattern is folded along a certain line and the two halves match perfectly. What is that line called with respect to the kolam?
questions.a: a line of symmetry of the kolam
o: a line of symmetry of the kolam
the centre of rotation of the kolam
an angle of symmetry of the kolam

questions.q: Consider: (I) Every line drawn through the middle of a figure is a line of symmetry. (II) A line of symmetry must make the two folded parts overlap exactly. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only II

questions.q: A blue triangle is folded along a dotted line and one half covers the other completely. A four-piece puzzle is folded along another dotted line, but the left half does not fit over the right half. Which figure has a line of symmetry along its dotted line?
questions.a: the blue triangle only

questions.q: A butterfly picture has 1 line of symmetry and a cloud picture has none. If you fold each along its stated symmetry, what would you expect?
questions.a: the butterfly's two halves match exactly; no fold makes the cloud's halves match
o: the butterfly's two halves match exactly; no fold makes the cloud's halves match
both match exactly along any fold
the cloud matches but the butterfly does not

questions.q: A rectangle (not a square) is folded first along the line joining the midpoints of its longer sides, and then along its diagonal. State, with a reason, whether each fold gives a line of symmetry.
questions.a: The fold joining the midpoints of the longer sides gives a line of symmetry because the two halves match exactly. The diagonal fold does not, because the two triangular halves are different shapes and do not overlap.

questions.q: State the number of lines of symmetry of (a) an equilateral triangle (all sides and angles equal) and (b) a triangle with no two sides equal.
questions.a: (a) An equilateral triangle has 3 lines of symmetry. (b) A triangle with no two sides equal (a scalene triangle) has no line of symmetry.

questions.q: Two dotted lines are drawn on a square: one is a diagonal, and the other joins the midpoints of a pair of opposite sides. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: both dotted lines are lines of symmetry of the square
o: both dotted lines are lines of symmetry of the square
only the diagonal is a line of symmetry
only the midpoint line is a line of symmetry
neither dotted line is a line of symmetry

questions.q: A rectangle (not a square) has one dotted line joining the midpoints of its shorter sides and another dotted line that is its diagonal. Decide which dotted line(s), if any, are lines of symmetry, and explain your reasoning for each.
questions.a: The line joining the midpoints of the shorter sides is a line of symmetry because folding along it makes the two halves overlap exactly. The diagonal is not a line of symmetry because folding along it does not make the two triangular halves match; a rectangle's diagonal is a line of symmetry only when the rectangle is a square.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A square has 4 lines of symmetry. Reason (R): Every quadrilateral has 4 lines of symmetry.
questions.a: A is true but R is false
o: A is true but R is false
both A and R are true and R explains A
both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is false but R is true

questions.q: A figure is folded along a line and the two halves DO NOT overlap. What can we correctly conclude?
questions.a: that line is not a line of symmetry of the figure
o: that line is not a line of symmetry of the figure
the figure has no line of symmetry at all

questions.q: A student claims: 'Since a square has 4 lines of symmetry and a square has 4 sides, every quadrilateral must have exactly as many lines of symmetry as it has sides.' Evaluate this claim using a rectangle that is not a square as a counter-example.
questions.a: The claim is false. A rectangle that is not a square has 4 sides but only 2 lines of symmetry (the lines joining the midpoints of opposite sides); its diagonals are not lines of symmetry, unlike a square's diagonals.

questions.q: A classmate folds a rectangle along its diagonal and says 'the halves almost match, so this is close enough to call it a line of symmetry.' Do you agree? Justify your answer.
questions.a: No; a line of symmetry must make the two halves overlap exactly, not almost. Since a non-square rectangle's diagonal does not give an exact overlap, it is not a line of symmetry.

questions.q: Design a quadrilateral (other than a square) that has exactly 2 lines of symmetry, and describe both lines.
questions.a: Sample answer: a rectangle that is not a square has exactly 2 lines of symmetry, the line joining the midpoints of the longer sides and the line joining the midpoints of the shorter sides; its diagonals are not lines of symmetry. Any correctly justified quadrilateral with exactly 2 valid lines of symmetry is acceptable.
s: Reasoning that the count is exactly 2

concepts.name: Multiple lines of symmetry and reflection
concepts.description: Some figures such as a square have more than one line of symmetry; reflecting a figure along a line of symmetry swaps corresponding points across that line.
concepts.idea: Folding a shape in different ways can reveal more than one line of symmetry, and each line of symmetry swaps the points on either side of it.
concepts.rule: A square has 4 lines of symmetry (the vertical and horizontal lines through its side-midpoints, and its 2 diagonals). Labelling a square's corners A, B, C, D clockwise from top-left: the vertical line of symmetry swaps A with B and D with C; the horizontal line of symmetry swaps A with D and B with C; the diagonal from A to C keeps A and C fixed and swaps B with D. This kind of symmetry is also called reflection symmetry.
concepts.example: Folding a square along its vertical, horizontal and both diagonal lines all give matching halves, so a square has 4 lines of symmetry; folding a (non-square) rectangle along its diagonal does not match.

questions.q: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?
When a figure is reflected along its line of symmetry so the two parts match, we say the figure has ____ symmetry.
questions.a: reflection

questions.q: A square's four lines of symmetry are the vertical line, the horizontal line, and
questions.a: both diagonals
o: only the horizontal line, counted twice

questions.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four lines of symmetry of a square?
questions.a: a line joining two adjacent corners
o: a line joining two adjacent corners
the vertical line through the midpoints of the top and bottom sides
the horizontal line through the midpoints of the left and right sides

questions.q: Square ABCD is labelled clockwise from top-left (A top-left, B top-right, C bottom-right, D bottom-left). Reflecting along the vertical line of symmetry sends corner A to the position earlier occupied by
questions.a: B

questions.q: In square ABCD (labelled clockwise from top-left), reflecting along the vertical line of symmetry sends corner D to the position earlier occupied by corner ____.
questions.a: C

questions.q: Reflecting square ABCD (labelled clockwise from top-left) along the diagonal from A to C sends corner B to the position earlier occupied by
questions.a: D

questions.q: Reflecting square ABCD (labelled clockwise from top-left) along its horizontal line of symmetry sends corner A to the position earlier occupied by
questions.a: D

questions.q: Consider a square ABCD (labelled clockwise from top-left). (I) Reflecting along the diagonal from A to C keeps A and C fixed. (II) Reflecting along the diagonal from A to C swaps B and D. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Both I and II

questions.q: A square has how many more lines of symmetry than a rectangle that is not a square?
questions.a: 2 more (4 versus 2)

questions.q: What does a line of symmetry do to the two parts of a figure on either side of it?
questions.a: it reflects each part exactly onto the other, like a mirror
o: it reflects each part exactly onto the other, like a mirror
it rotates each part by 90 degrees
it only touches the parts at one point

questions.q: Square ABCD is labelled clockwise from top-left. State the new position of corner C after reflecting along (a) the vertical line of symmetry and (b) the horizontal line of symmetry.
questions.a: (a) Reflecting along the vertical line sends C to D's old position. (b) Reflecting along the horizontal line sends C to B's old position.

questions.q: A dotted line is drawn through a square along one diagonal, and another dotted line is drawn through a rectangle (not a square) along one diagonal. State whether each dotted line is a line of symmetry, with a reason.
questions.a: The square's diagonal is a line of symmetry because folding along it makes the two triangular halves overlap exactly. The rectangle's diagonal is not a line of symmetry because its two triangular halves do not coincide when folded; a rectangle's diagonal is a line of symmetry only when it is actually a square.

questions.q: Square ABCD (labelled clockwise from top-left) is reflected along its horizontal line of symmetry. Which pair of corners swap positions?
questions.a: B and C

questions.q: Square ABCD is labelled clockwise starting at top-left with A. Trace what happens to all four corners when the square is reflected along the diagonal from B to D (instead of the diagonal from A to C). State which corners stay fixed and which corners swap, with reasoning.
questions.a: Reflecting along the diagonal from B to D keeps B and D fixed, because they lie on that diagonal; A and C, which lie on opposite sides of this diagonal at equal distances from it, swap positions with each other.
s: B and D identified as fixed
A and C identified as swapping
Reasoning about equal distance from the diagonal

questions.q: Assertion (A): Every line of symmetry of a square passes through its centre. Reason (R): A figure can have a line of symmetry that misses its centre.
questions.a: A is true but R is false
o: A is true but R is false
both A and R are true and R explains A
A is false but R is true
both A and R are false

questions.q: A square is reflected along a diagonal. Which of the following does NOT happen?
questions.a: all four corners change position
o: the two corners on the diagonal stay fixed
the two corners off the diagonal swap positions
the square as a whole looks unchanged

questions.q: A student says: 'A square and a rectangle that is not a square both have 4 sides and 4 right angles, so they must have the same number of lines of symmetry.' Analyse this claim by comparing their actual lines of symmetry and explaining the key difference that breaks the claim.
questions.a: The claim is false. A square has 4 lines of symmetry (2 through side-midpoints and 2 diagonals) while a non-square rectangle has only 2 (through the side-midpoints); the rectangle's diagonals fail because its two triangular halves are not mirror images of each other, unlike in a square where all four sides are equal.

questions.q: A classmate says 'since a square has 4 lines of symmetry, reflecting it along any one of its diagonals must send every corner to a different corner.' Do you agree? Justify using what actually happens when a square is reflected along a diagonal.
questions.a: No; reflecting a square along a diagonal keeps the two corners lying on that diagonal fixed (they map to themselves), and only the other two corners swap with each other.
s: Correct reasoning about the fixed corners

questions.q: Label a square A, B, C, D clockwise from top-left, and describe, in your own words, what happens to each corner under reflection along the horizontal line of symmetry. Then state which lines of symmetry a square that is drawn but NOT labelled would still have.
questions.a: Sample answer: with A top-left, B top-right, C bottom-right, D bottom-left, reflecting along the horizontal line of symmetry swaps A with D and B with C, since it flips the square top-to-bottom while keeping left and right sides in place. Regardless of any labelling, an unlabelled square always has exactly 4 lines of symmetry: the vertical and horizontal lines through the midpoints of its sides, and its two diagonals.
s: Correct general count of 4 lines regardless of labelling

concepts.name: Making symmetric figures by folding, cutting and punching
concepts.description: Ink-blot folding, paper folding-and-cutting, and punching holes in folded paper all produce symmetric figures whose fold line becomes a line of symmetry; the resulting pattern can be predicted, or the fold reconstructed from the result.
concepts.idea: Whatever is on one side of a fold gets mirrored onto the other side when the paper is unfolded.
concepts.rule: A single hole punched away from a fold, in paper folded once, appears as 2 holes placed symmetrically about that fold line. Folding twice (vertically then horizontally) before a single punch away from both folds gives 4 holes, one in each quarter. A hole punched exactly on a fold line is not duplicated by that particular fold.
concepts.example: One hole punched near a corner of a paper folded only vertically opens out to 2 holes, mirror images of each other across the vertical crease.

questions.q: In the ink-blot activity, paper is folded once and ink is dropped on one half before pressing the halves together. What does the fold line become in the resulting pattern?
questions.a: a line of symmetry of the ink pattern
o: a line of symmetry of the ink pattern
an angle of symmetry of the ink pattern
an irrelevant crease with no role

questions.q: In the paper folding-and-cutting activity, the fold line in the finished symmetric shape is always a ____ of symmetry.
questions.a: line

questions.q: A square sheet of paper is folded once and a single hole is punched through both layers, away from the fold. When unfolded, how many holes appear?
Which of these punching/folding facts is NOT true?
questions.a: punching a hole exactly on the fold line still produces two separate holes when unfolded
o: punching a hole exactly on the fold line still produces two separate holes when unfolded
a hole punched away from the fold line produces two holes symmetric about the fold
folding twice (vertically then horizontally) and punching once can give four holes
the fold line always becomes a line of symmetry of the punched pattern

questions.q: Paper is folded vertically and then horizontally (two folds), and a single hole is punched through all layers, away from both folds. How many holes appear when fully unfolded?
questions.a: 4, one in each quarter

questions.q: If a paper folded twice (vertically and horizontally) shows exactly one hole after unfolding, the hole must have been punched exactly at the ____.
questions.a: centre

questions.q: In the paper cutting activity, a folded sheet is cut along a dotted line. When the sheet is unfolded, the cut edge is symmetric about
questions.a: the fold line
o: the shorter edge of the paper

questions.q: A punched pattern was made using a SINGLE hole but still shows holes in more than one position when unfolded. What does this tell us about how the paper was folded?
questions.a: it was folded more than once, for example vertically and then horizontally
o: it was folded more than once, for example vertically and then horizontally
it was not folded at all
the hole was actually punched more than once

questions.q: Consider two folded-paper activities: (I) In the ink-blot activity, the fold line becomes a line of symmetry of the resulting blot. (II) In the punching activity, a hole punched away from a single fold line always produces exactly 2 holes when unfolded. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Both I and II

questions.q: A square sheet is folded only vertically, and a hole is punched near the top-right corner, away from the fold. When unfolded, where is the second hole?
questions.a: near the top-left corner, at the mirror position across the vertical fold
o: near the top-left corner, at the mirror position across the vertical fold

questions.q: A rectangular sheet is folded only horizontally and a single hole is punched away from the fold. When unfolded, the two holes lie
questions.a: symmetric about the horizontal fold line
o: symmetric about the horizontal fold line
symmetric about the vertical centre line

questions.q: A square sheet is folded twice, vertically then horizontally, and a single hole is punched exactly on the vertical fold line but not on the horizontal one. Describe the pattern of holes seen when the paper is fully unfolded, and explain why.
questions.a: Only 2 holes appear, one on each half formed by the horizontal fold, both lying exactly on the (now visible) vertical fold line, because a hole punched exactly on one fold line is not duplicated by that fold, only by the other fold.
s: Correct reasoning about the hole on the fold line

questions.q: A strip of paper is folded like a fan into 4 equal sections and a single hole is punched through all layers, away from every fold line. How many holes appear and what is their arrangement when unfolded?
questions.a: 4 holes appear, one in each of the 4 sections, spaced evenly along the strip, related to each other by reflection across each fold line.

questions.q: In the paper-cutting activity, a sheet folded once is cut so the cut passes through the fold line at one point and away from it at another. What can we say about the resulting hole's shape?
questions.a: it is symmetric about the fold line, with the fold-line point on the boundary of both halves
o: it is symmetric about the fold line, with the fold-line point on the boundary of both halves
it is not symmetric at all
it becomes two separate unrelated holes
it always becomes a perfect circle

questions.q: A square sheet is folded three times: vertically, then horizontally, then along a diagonal of the resulting smaller square. A single hole is punched through all layers, away from every fold line. Predict how many holes will appear when the paper is completely unfolded, and explain your reasoning step by step.
questions.a: Each fold can double the number of holes if the punch is away from that fold's line, so 3 folds can give up to 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 holes; each successive fold reflects the existing holes to new symmetric positions relative to that fold line.

questions.q: Assertion (A): A single hole punched exactly on a fold line still appears as 2 separate holes after unfolding. Reason (R): Every hole punched through a folded sheet always doubles in number after unfolding, regardless of its position.
questions.a: A is false and R is false
o: A is false and R is false
both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q: When trying to reconstruct how a paper was folded from its punched pattern, which clue would NOT help?
questions.a: the colour of the paper used
o: the colour of the paper used
the number of holes and how they are arranged
whether any hole lies exactly on a line of symmetry
the shape formed by joining the holes

questions.q: A punched pattern shows exactly 4 holes forming the 4 corners of a rectangle, with no hole on either the vertical or horizontal centre line of the paper. Analyse what this tells you about how the paper must have been folded before punching.
questions.a: The paper must have been folded exactly twice, once vertically and once horizontally, with the single punch placed away from both fold lines; each fold reflected the hole to a new position, giving 2 x 2 = 4 holes forming a rectangle around the original punch position.
s: Correct link to the rectangle shape of the 4 holes

questions.q: A classmate says 'the more times you fold the paper, the more holes you will always get, no matter where you punch.' Evaluate this statement, considering what happens if the punch lands exactly on a fold line.
questions.a: The statement is not always true; a hole punched exactly on a fold line is not duplicated by that particular fold, so folding more times does not always increase the hole count as much as expected. It depends on the punch's position relative to each fold line.
s: Correct judgement that the statement is not always true
Correct reasoning using a hole on the fold line

questions.q: Design a folding-and-punching plan (state the folds and where you would punch) that produces exactly 6 holes in the final symmetric pattern. Explain why your plan works.
questions.a: Sample answer: fold the paper into 3 equal fan-fold sections along parallel lines, then fold once more in half across all three sections, and punch a single hole away from every fold line; this gives up to 2 x 3 = 6 holes, since the half-fold doubles the 3 sections' worth of holes. Any correctly justified combination of folds giving exactly 6 holes is acceptable.
s: Clear explanation of why it works

concepts.name: Rotational symmetry and angle of symmetry
concepts.description: A figure has rotational symmetry if rotating it about a fixed centre by some angle strictly between 0 degrees and 360 degrees makes it look exactly the same; that angle is called an angle of symmetry.
concepts.idea: Spin the figure about its centre of rotation; if it ever looks unchanged before a full turn, it has rotational symmetry.
concepts.rule: 360 degrees is always an angle of symmetry for any figure, because a full turn always returns it to its starting position; but a figure has rotational symmetry only if it also looks unchanged at some smaller angle. A square's angles of symmetry are 90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees.
concepts.example: A paper windmill matches itself after a quarter turn (90 degrees), so 90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees are all its angles of symmetry, and it has rotational symmetry.

questions.q: The fixed point about which a figure is rotated is called the
questions.a: centre of rotation

questions.q: An angle through which a figure can be rotated to look exactly the same as before is called an ____ of symmetry.
questions.a: angle

questions.q: Which angle is always an angle of symmetry for every figure, no matter its shape?
questions.a: 360 degrees

questions.q: Which of these is NOT required for a figure to have rotational symmetry?
questions.a: the figure must also have at least one line of symmetry
o: the figure must also have at least one line of symmetry
there must be an angle strictly between 0 degrees and 360 degrees that maps the figure onto itself
there must be a fixed centre of rotation
rotating by that angle must make the figure look unchanged

questions.q: A paper windmill looks unchanged after a quarter turn (90 degrees) about its centre. What do we say about the windmill?
questions.a: it has rotational symmetry
o: it has neither kind of symmetry

questions.q: A figure has rotational symmetry only if some angle ____ 0 degrees and 360 degrees maps it onto itself.
questions.a: strictly between

questions.q: A figure comes back to its original shape only after a full 360-degree turn and at no smaller angle. What can we say about it?
questions.a: it does not have rotational symmetry
o: it does not have rotational symmetry
it has rotational symmetry with 1 angle
it has rotational symmetry with 2 angles

questions.q: A square is rotated 90 degrees about its centre and looks unchanged. It is rotated again by another 90 degrees (180 degrees total) and again looks unchanged. What are the square's full set of angles of symmetry, including the ones not yet mentioned?
questions.a: 90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees

questions.q: Assertion (A): Every figure has 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry. Reason (R): Rotating any figure by a full turn always returns it to its starting position.
questions.a: both A and R are true and R explains A
o: both A and R are true and R explains A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
both A and R are false

questions.q: A figure with 3 radial arms placed randomly, not evenly spaced, is rotated about its centre. At which angle(s) does it look unchanged?
questions.a: only at 360 degrees

questions.q: A strip pattern looks unchanged only after a full 360-degree rotation, never at 180 degrees. Does this strip have rotational symmetry?
questions.a: no, because 360 degrees is the only angle that works
o: no, because 360 degrees is the only angle that works
yes, because 360 degrees is an angle of symmetry
yes, because it has an angle of symmetry at 180 degrees

questions.q: A square ABCD is rotated 90 degrees about its centre. State where point A moves to (in terms of the other corners) and give the next angle at which the square again looks unchanged.
questions.a: Point A moves to the position earlier occupied by B, following the square's rotation pattern A to B to C to D to A every 90 degrees; the next angle of symmetry after 90 degrees is 180 degrees.
s: Correct position of A after 90 degrees

questions.q: A figure with 4 radial arms is placed at equal 90-degree intervals. List all its angles of symmetry, and state how many angles of symmetry it has in total.
questions.a: Its angles of symmetry are 90, 180, 270 and 360 degrees, so it has 4 angles of symmetry in total.

questions.q: A figure has rotational symmetry with angles of symmetry 180 and 360 degrees. If it is rotated by 90 degrees, what happens?
questions.a: it does not look the same, since 90 degrees is not one of its angles of symmetry
o: it does not look the same, since 90 degrees is not one of its angles of symmetry
it looks the same, since 90 degrees is half of 180 degrees
it looks the same, since 90 degrees is a quarter of 360 degrees
it depends on the figure's colour

questions.q: A figure looks unchanged after being rotated by 120 degrees about its centre. Using this single fact, work out at least two more angles (besides 120 degrees itself) at which the figure must also look unchanged, and explain your reasoning.
questions.a: Rotating twice by 120 degrees (240 degrees total) must also leave the figure unchanged, since applying an angle of symmetry twice keeps the figure looking the same; rotating three times (360 degrees total) also leaves it unchanged, since 360 degrees is always an angle of symmetry for every figure. So 240 and 360 degrees are two more angles of symmetry.

questions.q: A figure is rotated by 45, 90, 135, 180, 225, 270, 315 and 360 degrees, and it looks unchanged ONLY at 180 and 360 degrees. Which of these is a FALSE statement about this figure?
questions.a: it has 8 angles of symmetry
o: 180 degrees is one of its angles of symmetry

questions.q: Consider a figure whose only angles of symmetry are 180 and 360 degrees. (I) The figure has rotational symmetry. (II) The figure would also look unchanged if rotated by 90 degrees. Which is or are correct?
questions.a: Only I

questions.q: A student claims: 'A figure that has a line of symmetry must also have rotational symmetry, since both are types of symmetry.' Analyse this claim using an isosceles (non-equilateral) triangle, which has exactly 1 line of symmetry, as an example.
questions.a: The claim is false. An isosceles (non-equilateral) triangle has exactly 1 line of symmetry but no rotational symmetry, because rotating it by any angle strictly between 0 and 360 degrees about its centre never makes it look unchanged; its only angle of symmetry is 360 degrees, which by definition does not count as rotational symmetry.

questions.q: A classmate says 'if a figure has any angle of symmetry at all, it has rotational symmetry.' Evaluate this statement, keeping in mind that 360 degrees is always an angle of symmetry.
questions.a: The statement needs correcting; every figure always has 360 degrees as an angle of symmetry, but rotational symmetry requires an angle strictly between 0 and 360 degrees that also works, not merely having some angle of symmetry.
s: Correct judgement that the statement needs qualification
Correct reasoning citing the always-360-degrees fact

questions.q: Design a figure (describe it in words) that has rotational symmetry with exactly 3 angles of symmetry, and list those angles.
questions.a: Sample answer: a figure with 3 identical radial arms placed at equal 120-degree intervals around a centre has exactly 3 angles of symmetry: 120, 240 and 360 degrees. Any correctly justified figure with exactly 3 angles of symmetry is acceptable.

concepts.name: Angles of symmetry of radial-arm figures
concepts.description: For a figure made of n equally spaced radial arms, the angles of symmetry are the n whole-number multiples of 360 degrees divided by n; every figure's angles of symmetry are whole-number multiples of its smallest angle of symmetry, and the total number of angles of symmetry is called the order of rotational symmetry.
concepts.idea: Equally spaced arms divide the full turn into n equal parts, so rotating by 360/n each time keeps matching the figure.
concepts.rule: n equally spaced radial arms give angles of symmetry 360/n, 2 x (360/n), ..., up to 360 degrees. A whole-number smallest angle of symmetry is possible only when it is a factor of 360 (e.g. 45 degrees works since 8 x 45 = 360, but 17 degrees cannot since 360 is not a whole-number multiple of 17).
concepts.example: 5 equally spaced radial arms have angles of symmetry 72, 144, 216, 288 and 360 degrees, giving order of rotational symmetry 5; 7 equally spaced arms give a smallest angle of 360 divided by 7, which is 51 and 3/7 degrees, not a whole number.

questions.a: If the smallest angle is x, the angles of symmetry are x, 2x, 3x, and so on. Since 60 degrees is one of them and exactly two angles (x and 2x) are less than 60 degrees, 60 degrees must be the third multiple: 3x = 60 degrees, so x = 20 degrees. questions.q: A figure has order of rotational symmetry 8. Analyse whether it is possible for this figure to also have exactly 5 lines of symmetry, and explain what usually connects the order of rotational symmetry to the number of lines of symmetry for the regular, evenly-arranged figures seen in this chapter.
questions.a: For the regular, evenly-arranged figures in this chapter, such as regular polygons and evenly spaced radial-arm shapes, the order of rotational symmetry and the number of lines of symmetry are equal, so a figure with order 8 would be expected to have 8 lines of symmetry, not 5. concepts.name: Symmetry of circles and regular polygons
concepts.description: A circle has every angle as an angle of symmetry and every diameter as a line of symmetry; a regular polygon with n equal sides and angles has n lines of symmetry.
concepts.idea: The more evenly arranged a figure's parts are, the more lines and angles of symmetry it has, with the circle as the most symmetric figure of all.
concepts.rule: For a circle, every rotation about the centre and every diameter gives symmetry. A regular polygon with n sides has n lines of symmetry, equal to its order of rotational symmetry. The Ashoka Chakra's 24 spokes give it 24 lines and 24 angles of symmetry.
concepts.example: A regular hexagon (6 equal sides) has 6 lines of symmetry, while the circle it can be inscribed in has infinitely many.

questions.q: A student says: 'Since a circle has infinite lines of symmetry, any shape with a very large number of sides, like a regular polygon with 1000 sides, must also be a circle.' Analyse this claim.

A regular polygon with 1000 sides has exactly 1000 lines of symmetry and order of rotational symmetry 1000, both finite numbers, however large; it can only approach the look of a circle, which alone has infinitely many lines and angles of symmetry, at every possible angle and along every diameter. No polygon, however many sides, actually reaches that.
s: Correct reasoning that the polygon's symmetry stays finite
Correct distinction from the circle's infinite symmetry
